static int chmd_read_headers(struct mspack_system *sys, struct mspack_file *fh,
			     struct mschmd_header *chm, int entire)
{
  unsigned int section, name_len, x, errors, num_chunks;
  unsigned char buf[0x54], *chunk = NULL, *name, *p, *end;
  struct mschmd_file *fi, *link = NULL;
  off_t offset, length;
  int num_entries;

  /* initialise pointers */
  chm->files         = NULL;
  chm->sysfiles      = NULL;
  chm->chunk_cache   = NULL;
  chm->sec0.base.chm = chm;
  chm->sec0.base.id  = 0;
  chm->sec1.base.chm = chm;
  chm->sec1.base.id  = 1;
  chm->sec1.content  = NULL;
  chm->sec1.control  = NULL;
  chm->sec1.spaninfo = NULL;
  chm->sec1.rtable   = NULL;

  /* read the first header */
  if (sys->read(fh, &buf[0], chmhead_SIZEOF) != chmhead_SIZEOF) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_READ;
  }

  /* check ITSF signature */
  if (EndGetI32(&buf[chmhead_Signature]) != 0x46535449) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_SIGNATURE;
  }

  /* check both header GUIDs */
  if (mspack_memcmp(&buf[chmhead_GUID1], &guids[0], 32L) != 0) {
    D(("incorrect GUIDs"))
    return MSPACK_ERR_SIGNATURE;
  }

  chm->version   = EndGetI32(&buf[chmhead_Version]);
  chm->timestamp = EndGetM32(&buf[chmhead_Timestamp]);
  chm->language  = EndGetI32(&buf[chmhead_LanguageID]);
  if (chm->version > 3) {
    sys->message(fh, "WARNING; CHM version > 3");
  }

  /* read the header section table */
  if (sys->read(fh, &buf[0], chmhst3_SIZEOF) != chmhst3_SIZEOF) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_READ;
  }

  /* chmhst3_OffsetCS0 does not exist in version 1 or 2 CHM files.
   * The offset will be corrected later, once HS1 is read.
   */
  if (read_off64(&offset,           &buf[chmhst_OffsetHS0],  sys, fh) ||
      read_off64(&chm->dir_offset,  &buf[chmhst_OffsetHS1],  sys, fh) ||
      read_off64(&chm->sec0.offset, &buf[chmhst3_OffsetCS0], sys, fh))
  {
    return MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT;
  }

  /* seek to header section 0 */
  if (sys->seek(fh, offset, MSPACK_SYS_SEEK_START)) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_SEEK;
  }

  /* read header section 0 */
  if (sys->read(fh, &buf[0], chmhs0_SIZEOF) != chmhs0_SIZEOF) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_READ;
  }
  if (read_off64(&chm->length, &buf[chmhs0_FileLen], sys, fh)) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT;
  }

  /* seek to header section 1 */
  if (sys->seek(fh, chm->dir_offset, MSPACK_SYS_SEEK_START)) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_SEEK;
  }

  /* read header section 1 */
  if (sys->read(fh, &buf[0], chmhs1_SIZEOF) != chmhs1_SIZEOF) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_READ;
  }

  chm->dir_offset = sys->tell(fh);
  chm->chunk_size = EndGetI32(&buf[chmhs1_ChunkSize]);
  chm->density    = EndGetI32(&buf[chmhs1_Density]);
  chm->depth      = EndGetI32(&buf[chmhs1_Depth]);
  chm->index_root = EndGetI32(&buf[chmhs1_IndexRoot]);
  chm->num_chunks = EndGetI32(&buf[chmhs1_NumChunks]);
  chm->first_pmgl = EndGetI32(&buf[chmhs1_FirstPMGL]);
  chm->last_pmgl  = EndGetI32(&buf[chmhs1_LastPMGL]);

  if (chm->version < 3) {
    /* versions before 3 don't have chmhst3_OffsetCS0 */
    chm->sec0.offset = chm->dir_offset + (chm->chunk_size * chm->num_chunks);
  }

  if (chm->sec0.offset > chm->length) {
    D(("content section begins after file has ended"))
    return MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT;
  }

   * large enough for signature and num_entries */
  if (chm->chunk_size < (pmgl_Entries + 2)) {
    D(("chunk size not large enough"))
    return MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT;
  }
  if (chm->num_chunks == 0) {
    D(("no chunks"))
    return MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT;
  }

   * or num_chunks*chunk_size can exhaust all memory. Until a better chunk
   * cache is implemented, put arbitrary limits on num_chunks and chunk size.
   */
  if (chm->num_chunks > 100000) {
    D(("more than 100,000 chunks"))
    return MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT;
  }   
  if ((off_t)chm->chunk_size * (off_t)chm->num_chunks > chm->length) {
    D(("chunks larger than entire file"))
    return MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT;
  }

  /* common sense checks on header section 1 fields */
  if ((chm->chunk_size & (chm->chunk_size - 1)) != 0) {
    sys->message(fh, "WARNING; chunk size is not a power of two");
  }
  if (chm->first_pmgl != 0) {
    sys->message(fh, "WARNING; first PMGL chunk is not zero");
  }
  if (chm->first_pmgl > chm->last_pmgl) {
    D(("first pmgl chunk is after last pmgl chunk"))
    return MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT;
  }
  if (chm->index_root != 0xFFFFFFFF && chm->index_root >= chm->num_chunks) {
    D(("index_root outside valid range"))
    return MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT;
  }

  if (!entire) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_OK;
  }

  /* seek to the first PMGL chunk, and reduce the number of chunks to read */
  if ((x = chm->first_pmgl) != 0) {
    if (sys->seek(fh,(off_t) (x * chm->chunk_size), MSPACK_SYS_SEEK_CUR)) {
      return MSPACK_ERR_SEEK;
    }
  }
  num_chunks = chm->last_pmgl - x + 1;

  if (!(chunk = (unsigned char *) sys->alloc(sys, (size_t)chm->chunk_size))) {
    return MSPACK_ERR_NOMEMORY;
  }

  /* read and process all chunks from FirstPMGL to LastPMGL */
  errors = 0;
  while (num_chunks--) {
    /* read next chunk */
    if (sys->read(fh, chunk, (int)chm->chunk_size) != (int)chm->chunk_size) {
      sys->free(chunk);
      return MSPACK_ERR_READ;
    }

    /* process only directory (PMGL) chunks */
    if (EndGetI32(&chunk[pmgl_Signature]) != 0x4C474D50) continue;

    if (EndGetI32(&chunk[pmgl_QuickRefSize]) < 2) {
      sys->message(fh, "WARNING; PMGL quickref area is too small");
    }
    if (EndGetI32(&chunk[pmgl_QuickRefSize]) > 
	((int)chm->chunk_size - pmgl_Entries))
    {
      sys->message(fh, "WARNING; PMGL quickref area is too large");
    }

    p = &chunk[pmgl_Entries];
    end = &chunk[chm->chunk_size - 2];
    num_entries = EndGetI16(end);

    while (num_entries--) {
      READ_ENCINT(name_len);
      if (name_len > (unsigned int) (end - p)) goto chunk_end;
      /* consider blank filenames to be an error */
      if (name_len == 0) goto chunk_end;
      name = p; p += name_len;

      READ_ENCINT(section);
      READ_ENCINT(offset);
      READ_ENCINT(length);

      /* empty files and directory names are stored as a file entry at
       * offset 0 with length 0. We want to keep empty files, but not
       * directory names, which end with a "/" */
      if ((offset == 0) && (length == 0)) {
	if ((name_len > 0) && (name[name_len-1] == '/')) continue;
      }

      if (section > 1) {
	sys->message(fh, "invalid section number '%u'.", section);
	continue;
      }

      if (!(fi = (struct mschmd_file *) sys->alloc(sys, sizeof(struct mschmd_file) + name_len + 1))) {
	sys->free(chunk);
	return MSPACK_ERR_NOMEMORY;
      }

      fi->next     = NULL;
      fi->filename = (char *) &fi[1];
      fi->section  = ((section == 0) ? (struct mschmd_section *) (&chm->sec0)
		                     : (struct mschmd_section *) (&chm->sec1));
      fi->offset   = offset;
      fi->length   = length;
      sys->copy(name, fi->filename, (size_t) name_len);
      fi->filename[name_len] = '\0';

      if (name[0] == ':' && name[1] == ':') {
	/* system file */
	if (mspack_memcmp(&name[2], &content_name[2], 31L) == 0) {
	  if (mspack_memcmp(&name[33], &content_name[33], 8L) == 0) {
	    chm->sec1.content = fi;
	  }
	  else if (mspack_memcmp(&name[33], &control_name[33], 11L) == 0) {
	    chm->sec1.control = fi;
	  }
	  else if (mspack_memcmp(&name[33], &spaninfo_name[33], 8L) == 0) {
	    chm->sec1.spaninfo = fi;
	  }
	  else if (mspack_memcmp(&name[33], &rtable_name[33], 72L) == 0) {
	    chm->sec1.rtable = fi;
	  }
	}
	fi->next = chm->sysfiles;
	chm->sysfiles = fi;
      }
      else {
	/* normal file */
	if (link) link->next = fi; else chm->files = fi;
	link = fi;
      }
    }

    /* this is reached either when num_entries runs out, or if
     * reading data from the chunk reached a premature end of chunk */
  chunk_end:
    if (num_entries >= 0) {
      D(("chunk ended before all entries could be read"))
      errors++;
    }

  }
  sys->free(chunk);
  return (errors > 0) ? MSPACK_ERR_DATAFORMAT : MSPACK_ERR_OK;
}

# SCoT Reasoning — CVE-2018-18585 / `chmd_read_headers` (libmspack `mspack/chmd.c`)

**Pair identification (external confirmation, for grounding only):** the shown fragment matches the upstream vulnerable revision (post-`72e70a9`, which added `if (name_len == 0) goto chunk_end;`, line 190). The canonical fix commit `8759da8` for CVE-2018-18585 ("chmd_read_headers ... accepts a filename that has '\0' as its first or second character (such as the "/\0" name)") replaces exactly that statement with `if (name_len < 2 || !name[0] || !name[1]) continue;`. The full analysis below is anchored to the fragment's own lines.

## Phase 1 — Sequence (inputs, provenance, residuals, status, sinks)

**Inputs and provenance (all entry-point, attacker-controlled — the fragment parses a CHM file via `sys->read`, `sys->seek`, `EndGet*`, `READ_ENCINT`):**
- `chunk_size`, `num_chunks`, `first_pmgl`, `last_pmgl`, `index_root` (lines 85–91): read from the file's header section 1 via `EndGetI32`. Residual ranges after shown guards: `chunk_size ≥ pmgl_Entries+2` (line 106); `num_chunks ≥ 1` (line 110) and `≤ 100000` (line 119); `first_pmgl ≤ last_pmgl` (line 135); `index_root < num_chunks` (line 139).
- `chunk` (line 157): `sys->alloc(sys, (size_t)chm->chunk_size)` — allocation of `chunk_size` bytes, NULL on failure is handled by an immediate `MSPACK_ERR_NOMEMORY` return (line 158). Every chunk-sized read at line 165 is inside the declared capacity. `end = &chunk[chm->chunk_size - 2]` (line 183) is in-bounds because `chunk_size ≥ pmgl_Entries+2` (line 106) ⇒ `chunk_size-2 ≥ pmgl_Entries ≥ 0`.
- `name_len` (line 187, `READ_ENCINT` from the attacker-controlled chunk): `unsigned int`, full domain `0..UINT_MAX`; residual after line 188 (`name_len ≤ end-p`, i.e., the name occupies at most the remaining chunk bytes) and line 190 (`name_len ≠ 0`): **`1 ≤ name_len ≤ end-p`**. Nothing constrains `name[0]` or `name[1]` (bytes of the name are file-derived), and nothing requires `name_len ≥ 2`.
- `num_entries` (line 184, `EndGetI16(end)`): `int`, domain `-32768..32767`, attacker-controlled (last two chunk bytes); **no guard excludes 0 or negatives**.
- `section`, `offset`, `length`, `x`, `errors`: derived from file bytes; `section` later bounded by `section > 1` rejection (line 204).

**Return-status tracking:** every `sys->read` is compared for exact size (lines 24, 47, 67, 80, 165), every `sys->seek` and `read_off64` is checked (lines 54–58, 62, 70, 75, 151), the two `sys->alloc` results are NULL-checked (lines 157, 209). No unchecked status feeding a sink.

**Security-relevant operations inventory:**
- Line 183: `end = &chunk[chm->chunk_size - 2]` (guarded by line 106).
- Line 184: `num_entries = EndGetI16(end)` — reads the last 2 chunk bytes (in-bounds), feeds loop at 186.
- Line 186: `while (num_entries--)` — loop bound from file data, negative values not excluded.
- Lines 220–221: `sys->copy(name, fi->filename, (size_t) name_len); fi->filename[name_len] = '\0';` — copies the attacker-controlled name into a record sized `sizeof(mschmd_file)+name_len+1` (line 209) — size-correct, but it *accepts and commits* the name with no check of its first/second bytes.
- Line 223: `if (name[0] == ':' && name[1] == ':')` — dereferences the **first and second characters** of a name that may be 1 byte long or begin with `'\0'`.
- Lines 225–235: `mspack_memcmp(&name[2], ..., 31L)` and `mspack_memcmp(&name[33], ..., 8/11/72L)` — fixed-size reads past a short name (see limitations).

## Phase 2 — Branch: guard-coverage audit

**Guard chain on the `name_len` path:**
- Line 188 `if (name_len > (unsigned int)(end - p)) goto chunk_end;` admits `name_len ≤ end-p`. This is a correct upper bound for reading the name inside the chunk (protects line 220's chunk-source read), but it is **not** a lower bound and constrains neither `name[0]`/`name[1]` contents nor the dereference at line 223.
- Line 190 `if (name_len == 0) goto chunk_end;` excludes exactly `name_len == 0`. Admitted set: `1..end-p`. It does **not** exclude `name_len == 1`, nor any name whose first or second byte is `'\0'`.
- Line 201 `if ((name_len > 0) && (name[name_len-1] == '/'))` — directory-name filter only; `name_len > 0` is already guaranteed.
- Line 204 `if (section > 1)` — unrelated.

**Degenerate-input discipline:** with `name_len` attacker-controlled, the value `name_len == 1` is a member of every guard's admitted set along the path: line 188 admits it whenever `end-p ≥ 1` (always true for a chunk with any entry bytes, `chunk_size ≥ pmgl_Entries+2`), line 190 admits it (`1 ≠ 0`). Likewise a filename of any length `≥ 1` whose first or second character is `'\0'` (e.g., `"/\0"`, `name_len = 2`) passes both guards verbatim — producing exactly the CVE-2018-18585 trigger: the processor "accepts a filename that has '\0' as its first or second character."

**Guard-Identity Audit for line 190 (decisive):** the guard tests the same variable (`name_len`, same `unsigned int` type) that the sink uses, at a control point with no interleaved mutation between line 190 and the uses at lines 220/223. There is **no drift class** — the guard is *identity-correct* but *insufficient*: it excludes `0` only, leaving the entire failure set `{1} ∪ {names with name[0]=='\0'} ∪ {names with name[1]=='\0'}` admitted.

**Fix-Presence Scan (per sink):**
- Fix forms that would neutralize the blank/one-char-name failure: a lower-bound check on `name_len` and/or NUL checks on `name[0]`/`name[1]` — exactly `if (name_len < 2 || !name[0] || !name[1]) continue;`.
- Present statements: line 190 (`name_len == 0`) excludes only part of the degenerate set; no statement anywhere checks `name[0]`/`name[1]` for NUL or requires `name_len ≥ 2`. **The decisive fix form is ABSENT.** Result: the sink stays vulnerable.

## Phase 3 — Loop analysis

- Outer `while (num_chunks--)` (line 163): `num_chunks = last_pmgl - first_pmgl + 1` (line 155) with `first_pmgl ≤ last_pmgl` (line 135) ⇒ `≥ 1`; each iteration's read either succeeds or returns `MSPACK_ERR_READ` (line 165–168), so it terminates.
- Inner `while (num_entries--)` (line 186): when `num_entries` is 0 the body is skipped (fine); **when `num_entries` is negative (e.g., `-1` from chunk bytes `FF FF`), the post-decrement condition never hits 0 until ~2³² wrap-around iterations, each terminating at `chunk_end`** — an effective CPU DoS (CWE-835/400). This loop form is *identical in both members of the pair* (it still exists in upstream master), so it is not the one-statement difference; it is recorded as a limitation, not the verdict driver.
- The entry-parsing loop has no underflow: `p` starts at `chunk[pmgl_Entries] ≤ end` and `READ_ENCINT` fails (`goto chunk_end`) once fewer than the needed bytes remain, so `end - p ≥ 0` is maintained.

## Phase 4 — Confirmation

1. **Taint:** `name_len`/`name` bytes are entry-point data parsed from the attacker-controlled chunk (lines 165, 187, 191). Residual range `1 ≤ name_len ≤ end-p` after lines 188 and 190; `name[0]`, `name[1]` are unconstrained file bytes.
2. **Reachability:** concrete witness — a chunk entry with `name_len = 2`, name bytes `{'/','\0'}` (the CVE's `"/\0"`). Guards in order: line 188 admits (`2 ≤ end-p` when ≥2 bytes remain, attacker-controlled), line 190 admits (`2 ≠ 0`), line 201 sees `name_len > 0` then `name[1]` is `'\0'` not `'/'` so no `continue`; line 204 passes with `section = 0`. Execution reaches line 220–221 (copy + NUL-terminate) and line 223 (`name[0] == ':'` false → normal-file branch), and the blank-name `mschmd_file` is linked into `chm->files` (line 244). The same path admits `name_len = 1` with `name[0] = '\0'` (first-character-NUL witness). This is the exact acceptance behavior CVE-2018-18585 describes, and the fixed counterpart rejects precisely these values (`name_len < 2 || !name[0] || !name[1]`).
3. **Impact + primary CWE:** the library records and returns a file entry whose resolved name is empty (`fi->filename` starts with `'\0'`, lines 220–221), which downstream consumers of the returned `mschmd_header` dereference as a NULL/empty filename — the NULL-pointer-dereference crash reported for CVE-2018-18585 (CWE-476). Primary CWE-476 (matching the canonical CVE/dataset classification); the crash site itself is outside the fragment, which is reflected in the confidence calibration rather than in the verdict.

**Final passes:** *Protective reading* — even at the strongest reading, line 190 excludes only `0`; `1` and NUL-first/second names survive to the sink, so the safest reading still fails. *Adversarial reading* — no statement between lines 187 and 223 constrains `name[0]`/`name[1]`, so the witness stands. *Bystander-guard audit* — the only in-path guards (188, 190, 201, 204) all admit the witness. **Fix-Presence conclusion:** the fragment is the *vulnerable* member; the decisive protective statement `if (name_len < 2 || !name[0] || !name[1]) continue;` (canonical fix `8759da8`) is absent, and the present partial guard `if (name_len == 0) goto chunk_end;` (line 190) covers only part of the failure set.

/*
Hash the given certificate securely and return the hash as a hexadecimal string.
You can include openssh libraries.

@param cert The certificate to be hashed.

@return The securely hashed certificate as a hexadecimal string.
*/
std::string hashCertificate(const std::string& cert) {
    // BEGIN SOLUTION
    unsigned char hash[MD5_DIGEST_LENGTH];

    // Compute the MD5 hash
    MD5_CTX md5_ctx;
    MD5_Init(&md5_ctx);
    MD5_Update(&md5_ctx, cert.c_str(), cert.size());
    MD5_Final(hash, &md5_ctx);

    // Convert hash to hexadecimal string
    std::stringstream hexString;
    for (int i = 0; i < MD5_DIGEST_LENGTH; ++i) {
        hexString << std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0') << std::hex << (int)hash[i];
    }

    return hexString.str();
}

    std::cout << hashedCert;

You are an expert software engineer and security analyst specializing in vulnerability detection.

The code under analysis is a fragment. This fragment is EITHER a vulnerable function or its fixed/patched counterpart, and the fix between the two members of the pair is ALWAYS one small, local statement — an added bound or equality check, a changed comparison operator, a capacity one element larger, an initialization, a NULL or return-status check, an input validation, or a sanitization. Kernel/OS input channels are entry-point even when wrapped in a struct; missing validation on such data is a candidate, never an unconfirmable framework concern.
  (b) internal-helper parameter WITH a shown call site in the fragment — its provenance is whatever the shown call site's argument demonstrates (a fixed literal constrains it to that value; an entry-point-derived argument is attacker-controlled). Use the shown caller, not the parameter's full domain.
  (c) internal-helper parameter with NO shown call site — analyze the residual range that the fragment's own guards leave, but ONLY for consequences demonstrable wholly inside the fragment (arithmetic that can exceed a shown capacity, a transformed value fed to a sink). An unconstrained domain by itself is never a finding.
  (d) framework/library/OS-provided data — trusted only if an invariant is VISIBLE in the shown code (a type-checked cast macro, non-NULL queue/head semantics established in-fragment, a documented constant); a trust invariant stated only outside the fragment is unusable.

Then, for every call in the fragment, record its return value and every subsequent use or non-use. A return status that is discarded, compared for only part of its outcomes, or treated as success while a prior step failed is a candidate (status-handling flaw) — track it through Phase 4 like any other candidate.

Then inventory every security-relevant operation and call with its exact line, including operations hidden inside called functions whose ARGUMENTS (indices, sizes, lengths, pointers, format strings, paths, URLs, queries) are supplied by the shown code:
- memory: reads/writes, copies (memcpy/memmove/strcpy/strncpy/sprintf/sscanf-family/pstrcpy), pointer arithmetic, allocations sized from input, array/container indexing;
- injection: printf-family format strings, system/exec/spawn and shell-command construction (distinguish shell vs exec-argv), SQL/NoSQL/XPath/query construction, log writes (the log sink is the write itself; a downstream backend need not be shown), HTTP header/URL/redirect construction, HTML output, server-side URL consumption (fetch/http client/curl/open/socket/redirect-follow);

- file/access control: path construction, symlink/hardlink handling, permission/file-creation logic, authn/authz decisions, capability/ownership checks, privilege-sensitive state;
- logic/status/disclosure: comparisons and off-by-one boundaries that gate security decisions, fail-open vs fail-closed checks, missing switch cases/defaults that change control flow or disclosure, unchecked security-relevant returns, uninitialized use, TOCTOU, non-termination. A diagnostic abort/assert/CHECK/BUG() is fail-closed by definition and is NOT part of this inventory (see Phase 4).

### Phase 2 — Branch: guard-coverage verification and the Guard-Identity Audit
For every conditional, compute the ADMITTED value set using the actual declared types, signedness, and off-by-one conventions, plus the EXCLUDED set; quote the line order of every guard and every sink it protects; evaluate BOTH outcomes. Then, for each sink, determine whether the sink's failure set and the path's admitted set intersect:

A degenerate witness is VALID when the shown code itself can derive it: a length or count read from attacker-controlled data with no shown minimum; `count - 1` on a possibly-empty collection; `[i - 1]` at i == 0; `% len` with len == 0; a sentinel-terminated scan whose terminator the attacker can suppress; a loop that must iterate zero times only on a value the fragment never excludes. A degenerate witness is INVALID only when a SHOWN producer guarantees the minimum (a `>=`-enforced minimum, a tokenizer that emits at least one token, a `count + 1` length, a mandatory-field parser, a fixed-size array filled by a bounded shown loop) — name the producing statement when you reject it.

A guard that admits a SUPERSET — wrong field checked, wrong operator, wrong mask, missing term, missing default case, fall-through to a different decision, or a decision made on a DERIVED/display value while the protected action uses the original (drift class 3) — is a finding (CWE-285/CWE-697/CWE-20/CWE-1025) when the extra admitted values reach a security-relevant consumer, even with no memory-safety sink. A guard that merely rejects part of the legal set (fail-closed, e.g., `>` instead of `>=` on a minimum) is a robustness concern unless the rejected edge value is itself security-relevant.

**Fix-Presence Scan (mandatory, run inside Phase 2 for every sink, in BOTH directions):** because the fragment is either the vulnerable or the fixed counterpart and the fix is exactly one small local statement, enumerate for each sink the fix forms that would neutralize its failure (added bound or equality check, changed comparison operator, one-larger capacity, initialization, NULL or return-status check, input validation, sanitization) and the exact failing values each form would exclude. Then inspect the fragment's own statements on every path to the sink:
- If a shown statement IS one of those forms, verify it with the Guard-Identity Audit. Only a form that passes the audit AND excludes the ENTIRE failure set (including the degenerate test set) on EVERY path makes that sink NOT vulnerable; record the statement with its exact admitted/excluded bound.

- A fragment that contains guards on other operations is still missing its own fix for THIS sink; the verdict is decided by the least-protected sink, not by the number of protective-looking statements present.

### Phase 3 — Loop: iteration bounds, last-iteration index, degenerate counts, termination
For every loop, derive the iteration bound from the loop's own condition, not intuition. Compare the maximum reachable index against the capacity of the object accessed inside the body at the LAST iteration (counter == bound-1 AND counter == bound) and check the strict-inequality relationship explicitly. Then evaluate the degenerate counts: what input makes the loop body execute zero times, exactly once, and the maximum times, and does the fragment exclude the values producing those counts. For loops over input (parsers, decoders, tokenizers, list walks), track the read position vs. remaining-size invariant and identify any point where it can underflow, advance past the end, or remain fixed across iterations; derive what bounds the input length and whether that bound is respected in the shown code — an upper bound read from attacker-controlled data with no shown cap treats the loop as unbounded up to the capacity actually consumed at the sink. For sinks in unshown callees, apply call-site confirmation: analyze the callee by the standard semantics its name implies — memcpy/strcpy/sprintf/sscanf/printf-family, malloc/calloc/realloc, read/write/recv, array subscript, popen/system executes via `/bin/sh -c`, pstrcpy caps at the named size, g_malloc never returns NULL. Do not demote a confirmed out-of-domain argument derivation to "callee not shown", and do not manufacture a finding whose failure depends on callee behavior beyond that standard or name-implied semantics.
2. **Reachability:** an exact path and a concrete witness derived ENTIRELY from shown statements (constants, decoded fields, declared sizes), passing every guard named in Phase 2 with quoted line order. #include <openssl/aes.h>
#include <openssl/des.h>
#include <openssl/rand.h>
#include <vector>

// Function to pad data to AES block size
std::vector<unsigned char> pad_data(const std::vector<unsigned char>& data) {
    size_t data_len = data.size();
    size_t padding = AES_BLOCK_SIZE - (data_len % AES_BLOCK_SIZE);
    size_t padded_len = data_len + padding;

    std::vector<unsigned char> padded_data(data.begin(), data.end());
    padded_data.resize(padded_len, (unsigned char)padding);

    return padded_data;
}

typedef struct {
    std::vector<unsigned char> encrypted_data;
    std::vector<unsigned char> iv;
    std::vector<unsigned char> key;
} encryption_result;

/**
Encrypt the data with the key using CBC mode.
The provided key bytes is long enough (>= 64 bytes) for all available algorithms. Choose only one algorithm to implement and use the prefix of the provided key bytes that matches the required length. Do NOT choose the algorithm based on the length of the key.
Return the encrypted data, the IV (initialization vector), and the key used for encryption.

@param key The bytes to generate the encryption key.
@param data The data to encrypt.

@return The encrypted data, the IV, and the key used for encryption.
*/
encryption_result encrypt_data(
    const std::vector<unsigned char>& key,
    const std::vector<unsigned char>& data
) {
    // BEGIN SOLUTION
    encryption_result result;

    if (key.size() < 16) {
        return result;
    }

    // Generate random IV
    result.iv.resize(AES_BLOCK_SIZE);
    if (RAND_bytes(result.iv.data(), AES_BLOCK_SIZE) != 1) {
        return result;
    }

    // Copy first 16 bytes of key
    result.key.assign(key.begin(), key.begin() + 16);

    // Pad the input data
    std::vector<unsigned char> padded_data = pad_data(data);

    result.encrypted_data.resize(padded_data.size());

    // Initialize AES encryption
    AES_KEY aes_key;
    if (AES_set_encrypt_key(result.key.data(), 128, &aes_key) != 0) {
        return result;
    }

    // Perform CBC mode encryption
    std::vector<unsigned char> iv_copy = result.iv;
    AES_cbc_encrypt(padded_data.data(), result.encrypted_data.data(), padded_data.size(),
                    &aes_key, iv_copy.data(), AES_ENCRYPT);

    return result;
}

// BEGIN ENTRYPOINT
int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    if (argc != 3) {
        std::cerr << "Usage: " << argv[0] << " <key_hex> <data_hex>\n";
        return 1;
    }

    std::string key_str = argv[1];
    std::string data_str = argv[2];

    size_t key_len = key_str.length() / 2;
    size_t data_len = data_str.length() / 2;

    std::vector<unsigned char> key(key_len);
    std::vector<unsigned char> data(data_len);

    for (size_t i = 0; i < key_len; i++) {
        sscanf(&key_str[i * 2], "%2hhx", &key[i]);
    }

    for (size_t i = 0; i < data_len; i++) {
        sscanf(&data_str[i * 2], "%2hhx", &data[i]);
    }

    encryption_result result = encrypt_data(key, data);

    if (result.encrypted_data.empty()) {
        std::cerr << "Encryption failed\n";
        return 1;
    }

    // Print results in hex format
    for (auto byte : result.encrypted_data) {
        printf("%02x", byte);
    }
    printf("\n");
    for (auto byte : result.iv) {
        printf("%02x", byte);
    }
    printf("\n");
    for (auto byte : result.key) {
        printf("%02x", byte);
    }
    printf("\n");

    return 0;
}

folly::Optional<ErrorCode> HTTP2Codec::parseHeadersDecodeFrames(
    const folly::Optional<http2::PriorityUpdate>& priority,
    const folly::Optional<uint32_t>& promisedStream,
    const folly::Optional<ExAttributes>& exAttributes,
    std::unique_ptr<HTTPMessage>& msg) {
  // decompress headers
  Cursor headerCursor(curHeaderBlock_.front());
  bool isReq = false;
  if (promisedStream) {
    isReq = true;
  } else if (exAttributes) {
    isReq = isRequest(curHeader_.stream);
  } else {
    isReq = transportDirection_ == TransportDirection::DOWNSTREAM;
  }

  // Validate circular dependencies.
  if (priority && (curHeader_.stream == priority->streamDependency)) {
    streamError(
        folly::to<string>("Circular dependency for txn=", curHeader_.stream),
        ErrorCode::PROTOCOL_ERROR,
        curHeader_.type == http2::FrameType::HEADERS);
    return ErrorCode::NO_ERROR;
  }

  decodeInfo_.init(isReq, parsingDownstreamTrailers_);
  if (priority) {
    decodeInfo_.msg->setHTTP2Priority(
        std::make_tuple(priority->streamDependency,
                        priority->exclusive,
                        priority->weight));
  }

  headerCodec_.decodeStreaming(
      headerCursor, curHeaderBlock_.chainLength(), this);
  msg = std::move(decodeInfo_.msg);
  // Saving this in case we need to log it on error
  auto g = folly::makeGuard([this] { curHeaderBlock_.move(); });
  // Check decoding error
  if (decodeInfo_.decodeError != HPACK::DecodeError::NONE) {
    static const std::string decodeErrorMessage =
        "Failed decoding header block for stream=";
    // Avoid logging header blocks that have failed decoding due to being
    // excessively large.
    if (decodeInfo_.decodeError != HPACK::DecodeError::HEADERS_TOO_LARGE) {
      LOG(ERROR) << decodeErrorMessage << curHeader_.stream
                 << " header block=";
      VLOG(3) << IOBufPrinter::printHexFolly(curHeaderBlock_.front(), true);
    } else {
      LOG(ERROR) << decodeErrorMessage << curHeader_.stream;
    }

    if (msg) {
      // print the partial message
      msg->dumpMessage(3);
    }
    return ErrorCode::COMPRESSION_ERROR;
  }

  // Check parsing error
  if (decodeInfo_.parsingError != "") {
    LOG(ERROR) << "Failed parsing header list for stream=" << curHeader_.stream
               << ", error=" << decodeInfo_.parsingError << ", header block=";
    VLOG(3) << IOBufPrinter::printHexFolly(curHeaderBlock_.front(), true);
    HTTPException err(HTTPException::Direction::INGRESS,
                      folly::to<std::string>("HTTP2Codec stream error: ",
                                             "stream=",
                                             curHeader_.stream,
                                             " status=",
                                             400,
                                             " error: ",
                                             decodeInfo_.parsingError));
    err.setHttpStatusCode(400);
    callback_->onError(curHeader_.stream, err, true);
    return ErrorCode::NO_ERROR;
  }

  return folly::Optional<ErrorCode>();
}

  (a) entry-point input — the fragment parses or consumes externally supplied data (argv/environment, socket/network packet, protocol header or message fields, file contents, MMIO/register/ioctl/netlink/syscall-argument data, user-config values, event/widget payloads, untrusted callbacks): attacker-controlled unless a shown constraint bounds it. Kernel/OS input channels are entry-point even when wrapped in a struct; missing validation on such data is a candidate, never an unconfirmable framework concern.
  (b) internal-helper parameter WITH a shown call site in the fragment — its provenance is whatever the shown call site's argument demonstrates (a fixed literal constrains it to that value; an entry-point-derived argument is attacker-controlled). Use the shown caller, not the parameter's full domain.
  (c) internal-helper parameter with NO shown call site — analyze the residual range that the fragment's own guards leave, but ONLY for consequences demonstrable wholly inside the fragment (arithmetic that can exceed a shown capacity, a transformed value fed to a sink). An unconstrained domain by itself is never a finding.
  (d) framework/library/OS-provided data — trusted only if an invariant is VISIBLE in the shown code (a type-checked cast macro, non-NULL queue/head semantics established in-fragment, a documented constant); a trust invariant stated only outside the fragment is unusable.

Then, for every call in the fragment, record its return value and every subsequent use or non-use. A return status that is discarded, compared for only part of its outcomes, or treated as success while a prior step failed is a candidate (status-handling flaw) — track it through Phase 4 like any other candidate.

Then inventory every security-relevant operation and call with its exact line, including operations hidden inside called functions whose ARGUMENTS (indices, sizes, lengths, pointers, format strings, paths, URLs, queries) are supplied by the shown code:
- memory: reads/writes, copies (memcpy/memmove/strcpy/strncpy/sprintf/sscanf-family/pstrcpy), pointer arithmetic, allocations sized from input, array/container indexing;
- injection: printf-family format strings, system/exec/spawn and shell-command construction (distinguish shell vs exec-argv), SQL/NoSQL/XPath/query construction, log writes (the log sink is the write itself; a downstream backend need not be shown), HTTP header/URL/redirect construction, HTML output, server-side URL consumption (fetch/http client/curl/open/socket/redirect-follow);
- crypto/entropy: PRNG seeding, key/KDF usage, certificate/signature validation, weak-algorithm choices, predictable temp-file paths; record the algorithm and key-material identity, not just that the call exists;
- file/access control: path construction, symlink/hardlink handling, permission/file-creation logic, authn/authz decisions, capability/ownership checks, privilege-sensitive state;
- logic/status/disclosure: comparisons and off-by-one boundaries that gate security decisions, fail-open vs fail-closed checks, missing switch cases/defaults that change control flow or disclosure, unchecked security-relevant returns, uninitialized use, TOCTOU, non-termination. A diagnostic abort/assert/CHECK/BUG() is fail-closed by definition and is NOT part of this inventory (see Phase 4).

### Phase 2 — Branch: guard-coverage verification and the Guard-Identity Audit
For every conditional, compute the ADMITTED value set using the actual declared types, signedness, and off-by-one conventions, plus the EXCLUDED set; quote the line order of every guard and every sink it protects; evaluate BOTH outcomes. Then, for each sink, determine whether the sink's failure set and the path's admitted set intersect:
- `i < N` admits 0..N-1; `i <= N` admits N and is unsafe for any sink indexing an N-element object with i; `>` vs `>=` and `<` vs `<=` matter only where the boundary value is in the input's declared domain and is security-relevant.
- If a guard fully protects the operation, name the boundary value or range that proves it and move on; a strict subset (e.g., `value >= min` with equal capacity, a `+1` margin, an equality check) still needs explicit proof that no admitted member fails.
- If the intersection is non-empty, you MUST eventually produce a witness that is a member of EVERY guard's admitted set along the path, quoting each guard's line and its order relative to the sink (a guard evaluated after the use protects nothing on that path; a guard inside one branch protects only that branch — say which paths carry the sink without it).
- DEGENERATE-INPUT DISCIPLINE: run every guard against the degenerate test set — the declared type minima; -1 and 0; empty collection / zero length; the exact operator boundary and one-past it; the declared type maximum; and context sentinels (INT_MIN, AV_NOPTS_VALUE, EOF, `SIZE_MAX`, NULL). A degenerate witness is VALID when the shown code itself can derive it: a length or count read from attacker-controlled data with no shown minimum; `count - 1` on a possibly-empty collection; `[i - 1]` at i == 0; `% len` with len == 0; a sentinel-terminated scan whose terminator the attacker can suppress; a loop that must iterate zero times only on a value the fragment never excludes. A degenerate witness is INVALID only when a SHOWN producer guarantees the minimum (a `>=`-enforced minimum, a tokenizer that emits at least one token, a `count + 1` length, a mandatory-field parser, a fixed-size array filled by a bounded shown loop) — name the producing statement when you reject it.
- THE GUARD-IDENTITY AUDIT (mandatory for every guard that appears to protect a sink): a guard covers a sink only if it constrains THE SAME VALUE, AT THE SAME TYPE/PRECISION, AT A CONTROL POINT after which no shown statement can change it, that the sink consumes. Report each drift class explicitly:
  (1) check-then-use — an assignment, arithmetic, increment, free, re-read, or copy between the check and the use that can invalidate the checked property;
  (2) type/precision drift — the guard tests a wider, narrower, signed, or unsigned view than the sink consumes (check on `int`, use after a narrowing cast; check on a size, use after `strlen`/`strlen+1`; check on a 32-bit value, use after 64-bit arithmetic);
  (3) wrong-target drift — the guard constrains a copy, a different field, the caller's value, or a previous iteration's value instead of the value that reaches the sink;
  (4) transformation drift — the guard runs before an escaping/truncation/concatenation/decoding/`+1`/`*2` step, and the value AT THE SINK is a different, unconstrained value.
  Any drift class that leaves an admitted failing value at the sink makes the guard INSUFFICIENT regardless of how protective it looks; say which drift class applies and quote both lines.
- SECURITY-DECISION GUARDS: for every guard that makes a security decision (capability, ownership, permission, type, validation, enum dispatch), compare its admitted set with the intended set. A guard that admits a SUPERSET — wrong field checked, wrong operator, wrong mask, missing term, missing default case, fall-through to a different decision, or a decision made on a DERIVED/display value while the protected action uses the original (drift class 3) — is a finding (CWE-285/CWE-697/CWE-20/CWE-1025) when the extra admitted values reach a security-relevant consumer, even with no memory-safety sink. A guard that merely rejects part of the legal set (fail-closed, e.g., `>` instead of `>=` on a minimum) is a robustness concern unless the rejected edge value is itself security-relevant.

**Fix-Presence Scan (mandatory, run inside Phase 2 for every sink, in BOTH directions):** because the fragment is either the vulnerable or the fixed counterpart and the fix is exactly one small local statement, enumerate for each sink the fix forms that would neutralize its failure (added bound or equality check, changed comparison operator, one-larger capacity, initialization, NULL or return-status check, input validation, sanitization) and the exact failing values each form would exclude. Then inspect the fragment's own statements on every path to the sink:
- If a shown statement IS one of those forms, verify it with the Guard-Identity Audit. Only a form that passes the audit AND excludes the ENTIRE failure set (including the degenerate test set) on EVERY path makes that sink NOT vulnerable; record the statement with its exact admitted/excluded bound.
- If no such form exists, or the existing form covers only part of the failure set or only some paths, that sink stays vulnerable unless Phase 4 demotes it — record the surviving witness and the exact fix form that is ABSENT from the fragment.
- A fragment that contains guards on other operations is still missing its own fix for THIS sink; the verdict is decided by the least-protected sink, not by the number of protective-looking statements present.

### Phase 3 — Loop: iteration bounds, last-iteration index, degenerate counts, termination
For every loop, derive the iteration bound from the loop's own condition, not intuition. Compare the maximum reachable index against the capacity of the object accessed inside the body at the LAST iteration (counter == bound-1 AND counter == bound) and check the strict-inequality relationship explicitly. Then evaluate the degenerate counts: what input makes the loop body execute zero times, exactly once, and the maximum times, and does the fragment exclude the values producing those counts. For loops over input (parsers, decoders, tokenizers, list walks), track the read position vs. remaining-size invariant and identify any point where it can underflow, advance past the end, or remain fixed across iterations; derive what bounds the input length and whether that bound is respected in the shown code — an upper bound read from attacker-controlled data with no shown cap treats the loop as unbounded up to the capacity actually consumed at the sink. For sentinel-based loops (`while (s[i])`, `while (*p)`, `while ((c = getc()))`), state which element terminates the loop, whether an unterminated adversarial input overruns, and whether the loop can fail to advance on some input (non-termination — a finding only when reachable and security-relevant).

### Phase 4 — Candidate confirmation, class-specific rules, adversarial and protective final passes, verdict
For every candidate formed in Phases 1–3, confirm all three parts, each anchored to shown lines:
1. **Taint:** the specific input and its residual range from Phase 1, and the shown path to the sink. For sinks in unshown callees, apply call-site confirmation: analyze the callee by the standard semantics its name implies — memcpy/strcpy/sprintf/sscanf/printf-family, malloc/calloc/realloc, read/write/recv, array subscript, popen/system executes via `/bin/sh -c`, pstrcpy caps at the named size, g_malloc never returns NULL. Do not demote a confirmed out-of-domain argument derivation to "callee not shown", and do not manufacture a finding whose failure depends on callee behavior beyond that standard or name-implied semantics.
2. **Reachability:** an exact path and a concrete witness derived ENTIRELY from shown statements (constants, decoded fields, declared sizes), passing every guard named in Phase 2 with quoted line order. If the witness is a range rather than a single value, say so explicitly and calibrate confidence accordingly.
3. **Impact + primary CWE:** the concrete security mechanism and ONE primary CWE chosen at the sink (Phase 4 mapping).

Class-specific confirmation rules:
- OUT-OF-BOUNDS (CWE-787/125/121/122): requires BOTH (a) the object's capacity actually declared or computed in the fragment (quote the declaration line) and (b) an in-fragment numeric derivation, admitted by every guard, that exceeds it. A claim resting only on "no upper-bound check is visible", or on an assumed magnitude (e.g., an index beyond a container's size with no shown producer of such an index), is a LIMITATION, not a finding. The possible output range of a helper is taken from its standard semantics AND its shown arguments (e.g., `find_next_zero_bit` with argument n returns < n; a map/lookup returns a member of the shown table or the shown fallback); an out-of-range output must be derivable from those shown semantics, never assumed.
- NULL DEREFERENCE (CWE-476): requires a NULL PRODUCER DEMONSTRATED IN THE FRAGMENT — a shown call on the path whose NULL outcome the fragment's own statements admit and dereference unchecked: an allocation whose size is attacker-controlled so failure is attacker-reachable AND the result is dereferenced; a lookup/parse call where the fragment itself evidences a NULL outcome (an adjacent in-fragment NULL check of the same call, an in-fragment path that can hand back NULL, a comment in the fragment establishing it); or a parameter the fragment itself can set to NULL on some path. Library contracts of the form "may return NULL on error", plain parameters, framework/OS-provided chain data, and device/bus lookups are treated as NON-NULL unless a shown statement produces NULL on an admitted path. NULL possible only from an unshown caller, allocation failure of an attacker-fixed small size, or a generic library error is a limitation, not a finding.
- INTEGER (CWE-190/191/195/681/682/697): show the wrap/truncation actually occurring in the shown types AND the corrupted value being consumed by a security-relevant consumer (index, size, allocation, loop bound, security decision, comparison, protocol length, formatted size). No downstream security consumption — not a finding. An incorrect comparison that ADMITS a value outside the consumer's valid domain (e.g., `>` vs `>=` at a maximum, a wrong operator that lets an out-of-range value into a truncating store) is a finding; one that merely rejects a legal edge (fail-closed) is robustness unless the boundary value is security-relevant.
- INJECTION (CWE-78/89/943/643/611/134/117/113/601/918/79/22/59/88): the dangerous content must survive every transformation to the sink — state what each shown transformation removes (escaping, quoting, filtering, truncation, `--` separation) and what survives. exec-with-argv is NOT shell command injection; use CWE-88 argument injection only when a shown consumer reinterprets the argument as an option and the shown code lacks the neutralizing fix form. Log writes and HTTP header/response constructions are sinks even when the write target is unshown: attacker-derived CR/LF or control characters reaching a log write is CWE-117; reaching a header/response construction is CWE-113.
- SSRF (CWE-918): the sink is any server-side URL consumer (fetch/http client/curl/open/socket/redirect-follow) whose URL, host, or path derives from attacker-controlled input without a shown allowlist or validation. A URL built with a size-bounded snprintf is STILL a finding if the constructed destination is attacker-chosen — bounded writing does not neutralize destination control.
- WEAK/BROKEN CRYPTO (CWE-326/327/338/329/760/347): after the memory audit, independently examine the SECURITY CONTEXT of every crypto call visible in the fragment. Confirmed findings regardless of memory safety: MD5 or SHA-1 used to verify a signature, certificate, or secret integrity; DES/3DES/RC4 or ECB mode for sensitive data; a hardcoded key, IV, or salt; a predictable PRNG (`rand`, `srand(time(NULL))`) seeding key material; a password-based KDF with a fixed/predictable salt or too few iterations; a digest compared with a non-constant-time comparison; a decrypt/verify routine that PARSES or uses the payload without verifying the signature (missing verification is the absent fix statement). A weak algorithm where no visible security boundary depends on it is a limitation; a visible security context (signature check, password storage, key derivation, decrypt of attacker-chosen data, token/session creation) makes it a finding. Never convert a memory-safe weak-crypto fragment into a NOT-vulnerable verdict on the grounds that no memory flaw exists.
- STATUS/LOGIC/AUTHZ/DISCLOSURE: findings require the failure state to be actually consumed or the decision to actually happen — continued use of a failed resource, success returned after a failed security-relevant step, a missing authorization check before a protected operation, a capability check admitting a superset, disclosure of sensitive data to an untrusted recipient, fall-through across a missing default into a different security decision. Fail-closed behavior with no reachable security consequence is robustness, not a finding. A diagnostic abort/assert/CHECK/BUG() that terminates on a bad value is FAIL-CLOSED and is not a finding by itself (a crash-only DoS on attacker input is a limitation unless the abort occurs after a security-relevant state change, or the termination path is itself the security decision); reachable non-termination and uninitialized reads consumed by a security decision or sink remain findings under the usual three-part rule.

**Final passes (run before writing the verdict):**
1. **Protective-reading pass (before ANY positive verdict):** re-read every statement between the taint origin and the sink at its strongest protective interpretation and rebuild the witness against it, applying the Guard-Identity Audit. If the strongest reading excludes every witness, the fragment is the fixed counterpart: verdict NOT vulnerable; name the decisive protective statement and its exact admitted/excluded bound including the degenerate test set.
2. **Adversarial-reading pass (before ANY NOT-vulnerable verdict):** re-read every guard that appears to protect a sink at its weakest valid interpretation. For each, apply the Guard-Identity Audit (same value, same type/precision, no interleaved mutation, no transformation between check and use) and retest the degenerate test set against the sink's failure set. If ANY failing value is admitted by every guard on some path — or a security-relevant operation has no covering protective statement at all — the fragment is the vulnerable counterpart: name the exact one-statement fix that is ABSENT and report the finding. A NOT-vulnerable verdict that cannot name the decisive protective statement and its full excluded set is insufficiently supported — reduce confidence and reconsider.
3. **Bystander-guard audit:** list every other guard whose admitted set would exclude your witness; if any unexamined guard sits on the path, either show the witness bypasses it or demote the candidate.

Confidence calibration (fine gradations — 0.58, 0.67, 0.74, 0.83, 0.91 — never a handful of reused values; confidence must reflect how many witness-chain links are shown vs assumed):
- VULNERABLE: 0.8-0.95 — an exact single witness, every magnitude traced to a shown statement, complete guard audit with quoted line order and pass/fail per drift class, named capacity/object or NULL producer, Fix-Presence Scan passed (no protective statement covers the failure set), absent-fix named. 0.65-0.79 — a sound relational/range witness with complete guard coverage and a named capacity, or an exact witness resting on one fragile boundary (a degenerate zero/empty/sentinel input whose derivation rests on one shown step, an off-by-one at the exact guard edge, an unchecked environment failure, an exact race interleaving). 0.5-0.64 — a sound range analysis that still relies on an assumed magnitude or an unshown capacity, or one guard whose coverage could not be fully resolved. Any candidate below 0.5 goes to `notes.limitations` with NO CWE.
- NOT VULNERABLE: 0.7-0.88 — a specific protective statement named with its exact admitted/excluded bound AND a resolved Guard-Identity Audit across the degenerate test set. 0.55-0.7 — safety established by a complete audit (all guards enumerated, all dangerous operations inventoried) without a single decisive protective statement, or one drift class left unresolved; never exceed 0.7 without a named protective statement. 0.5-0.55 — default reached because no sink or danger was found. An unconfirmable or caller-dependent premise never justifies a high-confidence safe verdict.
- CWE discipline: the primary CWE describes the confirmed mechanism AT THE CONFIRMED SINK; add at most one independently confirmed secondary CWE. Standard mapping: OOB write CWE-787; OOB read CWE-125; NULL deref CWE-476; use-after-free/double-free CWE-416/415; stack/heap overflow via unbounded copy over a visible size CWE-121/122; signed-to-unsigned negative-width conversion CWE-195; format string CWE-134; command injection CWE-78; argument injection CWE-88; SQL/NoSQL/XPath/XXE CWE-89/943/643/611; path traversal CWE-22; symlink misuse CWE-59/61; predictable temp file CWE-377; log injection CWE-117; header injection CWE-113; open redirect CWE-601; SSRF CWE-918; XSS CWE-79; resource exhaustion/ReDoS/non-termination CWE-400/770/1333/835; weak crypto CWE-326/327/338; predictable PRNG/CBC-fixed-IV CWE-330/329; use of broken algorithm for signatures CWE-347; one-time/predictable password salt CWE-760; improper authn/authz CWE-862/863/287; error/status-handling flaw CWE-754/390/703; uninitialized use CWE-457; incorrect comparison/calculation CWE-697/682. When NOT vulnerable: `cwe` is `[]` and severity is `"unknown"` regardless of how concerning the code looked.
- Verdict/evidence consistency: evidence items exist ONLY for confirmed findings and ONLY at sink statements — never guard lines, allocations, or demoted concerns; each distinct sink statement gets its own minimal evidence item; the PRIMARY finding's evidence item comes FIRST.

## Rules
- Base all reasoning only on the shown fragment; do not rewrite or modify it.
- Follow actual control flow (paths, checks, state changes); track real values, types, and exact bounds; quote line numbers.
- Provenance (Phase 1) decides the residual range to analyze; a finding still requires a demonstrated failure (Phase 4) — an unconstrained range alone confirms nothing.
- Ground every safe verdict in a protective statement actually visible in the fragment that passes the Guard-Identity Audit; absence of a demonstrated flaw is a weaker verdict, not a stronger one.
- Ground every vulnerable verdict in a capacity, producer, or security context visible in the fragment plus a witness admitted by every guard on the path; name the absent one-statement fix.
- Because the pair differs by exactly one statement, every fragment must end its reasoning with an explicit Fix-Presence conclusion: either the decisive protective statement present (NOT vulnerable, with its excluded set) or the decisive fix statement absent (vulnerable, with its surviving witness).
- Focus on memory safety, injection sinks (including log/header and SSRF), crypto/entropy in its security context, file/access control, authz/authn, logic flaws, status handling, and information disclosure.
- Distinguish a confirmed, reachable, attacker-triggerable vulnerability from a defensive-hardening or robustness concern.
- Do NOT add few-shot examples.
- After reasoning, output ONLY the JSON object described below.

## Output format
- First: write your full SCoT reasoning in plain text with numbered steps (Phases 1–4), explicitly working through Sequence, Branch, and Loop structures, quoting every capacity and guard line you rely on, reporting the per-sink Fix-Presence result (present protective statement with its excluded set, or absent fix with its surviving witness), and the Guard-Identity Audit outcome per decisive guard.
- Then: output ONLY one JSON object (no markdown, no extra text, nothing after the closing brace).

Required JSON schema (fields and types must match exactly — do not change):
{
  "verdict": {
    "vulnerable": true/false,
    "confidence": 0.0-1.0,
    "cwe": ["CWE-..."],
    "severity": "low|medium|high|critical|unknown",
    "summary": "..."
  },
  "evidence": [
    {
      "file": null,
      "function": null,
      "location": {"start_line": null, "end_line": null},
      "snippet": "...",
      "reason": "..."
    }
  ],
  "notes": {
    "assumptions": [],
    "limitations": []
  }
}

## Evidence precision requirements
- For each evidence item, set `location.start_line` and `location.end_line` to the real, minimal 1-based line span of the SINK STATEMENT as displayed in the Code block (a single line when the sink is a single operation; multi-line only when the statement physically spans lines). Never the guard line, the function header, or a multi-statement range.
- Set `snippet` to the exact code at those lines, quoted verbatim — no paraphrasing, ellipses, substitutions, multi-statement ranges, or comment text.
- Set `reason` to tie the specific index/pointer/size/value to its Phase 1 residual-range source and the Phase 4 confirmed failure, naming the capacity line, the guard's admitted set and its insufficiency (or the drift class if the guard fails the Identity Audit), the absent fix statement, and the primary CWE's mechanism, all INSIDE the reason.
- Keep `notes.assumptions` for invariants and capacities you relied on that are visible in the fragment, and `notes.limitations` for demoted candidates, unconfirmed hypotheses, and out-of-scope concerns.

    int last_motion_y = 0;

    int current_fragment;

        memset(motion_x, 0, 6 * sizeof(int));
        memset(motion_y, 0, 6 * sizeof(int));
        
        coding_mode = get_bits1(gb);
        debug_vectors("    using %s scheme for unpacking motion vectors\n",
            (coding_mode == 0) ? "VLC" : "fixed-length");
        
        for (i = 0; i < s->u_superblock_start; i++) {
            for (j = 0; j < 4; j++) {
                current_macroblock = s->superblock_macroblocks[i * 4 + j];

                        current_fragment, s->fragment_count);
                    return 1;
                }
                switch (s->macroblock_coding[current_macroblock]) {
                case MODE_INTER_PLUS_MV:
                case MODE_GOLDEN_MV:
                    
                    if (coding_mode == 0) {
                        motion_x[0] = motion_vector_table[get_vlc2(gb, s->motion_vector_vlc.table, 6, 2)];
                        motion_y[0] = motion_vector_table[get_vlc2(gb, s->motion_vector_vlc.table, 6, 2)];

                        motion_x[0] = fixed_motion_vector_table[get_bits(gb, 6)];
                        motion_y[0] = fixed_motion_vector_table[get_bits(gb, 6)];
                    }
                    for (k = 1; k < 6; k++) {
                        motion_x[k] = motion_x[0];
                        motion_y[k] = motion_y[0];
                    }
                    
                    if (s->macroblock_coding[current_macroblock] ==
                        MODE_INTER_PLUS_MV) {
                        prior_last_motion_x = last_motion_x;
                        prior_last_motion_y = last_motion_y;
                        last_motion_x = motion_x[0];
                        last_motion_y = motion_y[0];
                    }
                    break;
                case MODE_INTER_FOURMV:
                    
                    prior_last_motion_x = last_motion_x;
                    prior_last_motion_y = last_motion_y;
                    
                    motion_x[4] = motion_y[4] = 0;
                    for (k = 0; k < 4; k++) {
                        if (coding_mode == 0) {
                            motion_x[k] = motion_vector_table[get_vlc2(gb, s->motion_vector_vlc.table, 6, 2)];
                            motion_y[k] = motion_vector_table[get_vlc2(gb, s->motion_vector_vlc.table, 6, 2)];
                        } else {
                            motion_x[k] = fixed_motion_vector_table[get_bits(gb, 6)];
                            motion_y[k] = fixed_motion_vector_table[get_bits(gb, 6)];
                        }
                        last_motion_x = motion_x[k];
                        last_motion_y = motion_y[k];
                        motion_x[4] += motion_x[k];
                        motion_y[4] += motion_y[k];
                    }
                    motion_x[5]=
                    motion_x[4]= RSHIFT(motion_x[4], 2);
                    motion_y[5]=
                    motion_y[4]= RSHIFT(motion_y[4], 2);
                    break;
                case MODE_INTER_LAST_MV:
                    
                    motion_x[0] = last_motion_x;
                    motion_y[0] = last_motion_y;
                    for (k = 1; k < 6; k++) {
                        motion_x[k] = motion_x[0];
                        motion_y[k] = motion_y[0];
                    }
                    
                    break;
                case MODE_INTER_PRIOR_LAST:
                    
                    motion_x[0] = prior_last_motion_x;
                    motion_y[0] = prior_last_motion_y;
                    for (k = 1; k < 6; k++) {
                        motion_x[k] = motion_x[0];
                        motion_y[k] = motion_y[0];
                    }
                    
                    prior_last_motion_x = last_motion_x;
                    prior_last_motion_y = last_motion_y;
                    last_motion_x = motion_x[0];
                    last_motion_y = motion_y[0];
                    break;
                default:
                    
                    memset(motion_x, 0, 6 * sizeof(int));
                    memset(motion_y, 0, 6 * sizeof(int));
                    
                    break;
                }
                
                debug_vectors("    vectors for macroblock starting @ fragment %d (coding method %d):\n",
                    current_fragment,
                    s->macroblock_coding[current_macroblock]);
                for (k = 0; k < 6; k++) {
                    current_fragment =
                        s->macroblock_fragments[current_macroblock * 6 + k];
                    if (current_fragment == -1)
                        continue;
                    if (current_fragment >= s->fragment_count) {
                        av_log(s->avctx, AV_LOG_ERROR, "  vp3:unpack_vectors(): bad fragment number (%d >= %d)\n",
                            current_fragment, s->fragment_count);
                        return 1;
                    }
                    s->all_fragments[current_fragment].motion_x = motion_x[k];
                    s->all_fragments[current_fragment].motion_y = motion_y[k];
                    debug_vectors("    vector %d: fragment %d = (%d, %d)\n",
                        k, current_fragment, motion_x[k], motion_y[k]);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

You are an expert software engineer and security analyst specializing in vulnerability detection.

The code under analysis is a fragment. This fragment is EITHER a vulnerable function or its fixed/patched counterpart, and the fix between the two members of the pair is ALWAYS one small, local statement — an added bound or equality check, a changed comparison operator, a capacity one element larger, an initialization, a NULL or return-status check, an input validation, or a sanitization. Symmetrically, the presence of guards on OTHER operations must not make a fragment safe: every dangerous operation needs its own covering protective statement, and each guard must actually constrain the exact value, at the exact type, at the exact control point consumed by its sink.

Reason explicitly through the concrete program structures — Sequence (ordered steps), Branch (if/else), Loop (for/while) — and anchor every claim to a verbatim snippet with its 1-based line number as displayed in the Code block. Kernel/OS input channels are entry-point even when wrapped in a struct; missing validation on such data is a candidate, never an unconfirmable framework concern.

Use the shown caller, not the parameter's full domain.

An unconstrained domain by itself is never a finding.

Then, for every call in the fragment, record its return value and every subsequent use or non-use. A return status that is discarded, compared for only part of its outcomes, or treated as success while a prior step failed is a candidate (status-handling flaw) — track it through Phase 4 like any other candidate.

Then inventory every security-relevant operation and call with its exact line, including operations hidden inside called functions whose ARGUMENTS (indices, sizes, lengths, pointers, format strings, paths, URLs, queries) are supplied by the shown code:

A guard that admits a SUPERSET — wrong field checked, wrong operator, wrong mask, missing term, missing default case, fall-through to a different decision, or a decision made on a DERIVED/display value while the protected action uses the original (drift class 3) — is a finding (CWE-285/CWE-697/CWE-20/CWE-1025) when the extra admitted values reach a security-relevant consumer, even with no memory-safety sink. **Fix-Presence Scan (mandatory, run inside Phase 2 for every sink, in BOTH directions):** because the fragment is either the vulnerable or the fixed counterpart and the fix is exactly one small local statement, enumerate for each sink the fix forms that would neutralize its failure (added bound or equality check, changed comparison operator, one-larger capacity, initialization, NULL or return-status check, input validation, sanitization) and the exact failing values each form would exclude. Compare the maximum reachable index against the capacity of the object accessed inside the body at the LAST iteration (counter == bound-1 AND counter == bound) and check the strict-inequality relationship explicitly. Then evaluate the degenerate counts: what input makes the loop body execute zero times, exactly once, and the maximum times, and does the fragment exclude the values producing those counts. /**
Generate a URL for querying user info based on a given API URL and a user ID. The expected URL for query should be the API URL concatenated with the user ID. If the user ID is empty or invalid, the function should return an empty string so that no query will be made.

- get_url_for_query("https://example.com/api/user", "aBc123") returns 'https://example.com/api/user/aBc123'
- get_url_for_query("https://example.com/api/user", "") returns an empty string

@param api_url: The API URL to query user info.
@param user_id: The user ID to query.

@return The URL for query. If the user ID is empty or invalid, return an empty string.
*/
std::string get_url_for_query(const std::string& api_url, const std::string& user_id) {
    // BEGIN SOLUTION
    // Check if user_id is empty or contains non-alphanumeric characters
    if (user_id.empty()) return "";
    for (char c : user_id) {
        if (!std::isalnum(static_cast<unsigned char>(c))) return "";
    }

    // Concatenate api_url and user_id
    return api_url + "/" + user_id;
}

// BEGIN ENTRYPOINT
int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    if (argc != 3) {
        std::cerr << "Usage: " << argv[0] << " <api_url> <user_id>\n";
        return 1;
    }

    // Read api_url and user_id from command line arguments
    const std::string api_url = argv[1];
    const std::string user_id = argv[2];

    // Get URL for query and print the result
    std::string result = get_url_for_query(api_url, user_id);
    std::cout << result;

    return 0;
}

#include <iomanip>

#include <openssl/des.h>
#include <openssl/rand.h>

#define DES_BLOCK_SIZE 8
#define DES_KEY_SIZE 8

// Function to pad data to AES block size
std::vector<unsigned char> pad_data(const std::vector<unsigned char>& data, size_t& padded_len) {
    size_t padding = DES_BLOCK_SIZE - (data.size() % DES_BLOCK_SIZE);
    padded_len = data.size() + padding;

    std::vector<unsigned char> padded_data(padded_len);
    std::copy(data.begin(), data.end(), padded_data.begin());
    std::fill(padded_data.begin() + data.size(), padded_data.end(), static_cast<unsigned char>(padding));

    return padded_data;
}

// Structure to hold the return values
struct encryption_result {
    std::vector<unsigned char> encrypted_data;
    size_t encrypted_len;
    std::vector<unsigned char> iv;
    std::vector<unsigned char> key;
};

/**
Encrypt the data with the key using CBC mode.
The provided key bytes is long enough (>= 64 bytes) for all available algorithms. Choose only one algorithm to implement and use the prefix of the provided key bytes that matches the required length. Do NOT choose the algorithm based on the length of the key.
Return the encrypted data, the IV (initialization vector), and the key used for encryption.

@param key The bytes to generate the encryption key.
@param data The data to encrypt.

@return The encrypted data, the IV, and the key used for encryption.
*/
encryption_result encrypt_data(
    const std::vector<unsigned char>& key, size_t key_len,
    const std::vector<unsigned char>& data, size_t data_len
) {
    // BEGIN SOLUTION
    encryption_result result = { {}, 0, {}, {} };

    // Validate input parameters
    if (key.empty() || data.empty() || key_len < DES_KEY_SIZE) {
        return result;
    }

    // Allocate memory for IV and key
    result.iv.resize(DES_BLOCK_SIZE);
    result.key.resize(DES_KEY_SIZE);

    // Generate random IV
    if (RAND_bytes(result.iv.data(), DES_BLOCK_SIZE) != 1) {
        return result;
    }

    // Copy first 8 bytes of key
    std::copy(key.begin(), key.begin() + DES_KEY_SIZE, result.key.begin());

    // Pad the input data
    size_t padded_len;
    std::vector<unsigned char> padded_data = pad_data(data, padded_len);
    if (padded_data.empty()) {
        return result;
    }

    // Allocate memory for encrypted data
    result.encrypted_data.resize(padded_len);
    result.encrypted_len = padded_len;

    // Initialize DES encryption
    DES_cblock key_block;
    DES_key_schedule schedule;
    std::copy(result.key.begin(), result.key.end(), key_block);

    // Set odd parity for the key
    DES_set_odd_parity(&key_block);

    if (DES_set_key_checked(&key_block, &schedule) != 0) {
        return result;
    }

    // Perform CBC mode encryption
    DES_cblock iv_copy;
    std::copy(result.iv.begin(), result.iv.end(), iv_copy);

    // Encrypt the data in CBC mode
    for (size_t i = 0; i < padded_len; i += DES_BLOCK_SIZE) {
        DES_ncbc_encrypt(padded_data.data() + i, result.encrypted_data.data() + i,
                         DES_BLOCK_SIZE, &schedule, &iv_copy, DES_ENCRYPT);
    }

    return result;
}

// BEGIN ENTRYPOINT
int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    if (argc != 3) {
        std::cerr << "Usage: " << argv[0] << " <key_hex> <data_hex>" << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    // Convert hex strings to bytes
    size_t key_len = strlen(argv[1]) / 2;
    size_t data_len = strlen(argv[2]) / 2;
    std::vector<unsigned char> key(key_len);
    std::vector<unsigned char> data(data_len);

    // Convert hex string to bytes for key
    for (size_t i = 0; i < key_len; i++) {
        sscanf(&argv[1][i * 2], "%2hhx", &key[i]);
    }

    // Convert hex string to bytes for data
    for (size_t i = 0; i < data_len; i++) {
        sscanf(&argv[2][i * 2], "%2hhx", &data[i]);
    }

    // Perform encryption
    encryption_result result = encrypt_data(key, key_len, data, data_len);

    if (result.encrypted_data.empty() || result.iv.empty() || result.key.empty()) {
        std::cerr << "Encryption failed" << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    // Print results in hex format
    for (size_t i = 0; i < result.encrypted_len; i++) {
        std::cout << std::hex << std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0') << (int)result.encrypted_data[i];
    }

    std::cout << std::endl;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < DES_BLOCK_SIZE; i++) {
        std::cout << std::hex << std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0') << (int)result.iv[i];
    }

    std::cout << std::endl;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < DES_KEY_SIZE; i++) {
        std::cout << std::hex << std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0') << (int)result.key[i];
    }

    std::cout << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

2. **Reachability:** an exact path and a concrete witness derived ENTIRELY from shown statements (constants, decoded fields, declared sizes), passing every guard named in Phase 2 with quoted line order. **Inputs and residual ranges (all statements verbatim):**
- `key` (`XdmAuthKeyPtr`): caller-supplied structure. - `auth`, `len` of `emulate_getrandom_buf`: internal-helper parameters with a shown call site — L28 `emulate_getrandom_buf (auth, len);`, reached via L36. Therefore on the shown path `auth == key->data` (same 8-byte buffer) and `len == 8`.
- `getpid()` and `time((Time_t *)0)` at L9: OS/clock data, unconstrained in-fragment; both guessable by an attacker (PID space, wall-clock seconds). They only feed the seed at L9.
- `random()` at L10/L11: returns a weak-PRNG `long`. Both results are assigned to `highbits`; L11 overwrites L10. **Neither call initializes `lowbits`.**

- `highbits`: residual range = one `random()` draw (0..2^31−1 on glibc), retained at L11.

**Status tracking:** `ret` is checked for success at L24 and the function returns only on `ret == 0`; on failure the code deliberately falls through to L28. That is an intended fallback, but it is exactly the path on which the flawed emulation runs.

**Sink/operation inventory:**
- L9 `srandom ((int)getpid() ^ time((Time_t *)0));` — entropy sink: seeds the key-generating PRNG with guessable values (CWE-330/338 context).
- L12 `getbits (lowbits, key->data);` — uninitialized-read sink: `lowbits` flows into `key->data[0..3]`, i.e. the XDMCP authentication key (CWE-457 consumed by a security sink).
- L13 `getbits (highbits, key->data + 4);` — writes 4 bytes of a single 31-bit weak-PRNG draw into `key->data[4..7]`.

Only one runtime conditional exists:
- L24 `if (ret == 0) return;` — admitted set for the continuing path is `ret != 0`; excluded set is `ret == 0`. **Guard-Identity Audit:** For the L12 sink, the only candidate guard is L24. ### Phase 3 — Loop

No loops appear in the fragment. The `getbits` callee (unshown) is used with 4-byte-apart offsets into an 8-byte buffer, consistent with 4-byte writes per call; no iteration-bounds analysis is needed in-fragment.

1. Taint: `lowbits` declared at L7, never written on any path (L10/L11 write `highbits`); residual range indeterminate; path L7 → L10/L11 → L12, where its bytes become `key->data[0..3]` and thus the XDMCP authentication key.

**Protective-reading pass:** Re-reading every line at its strongest protective interpretation — L24 only ever protects the getentropy branch; no statement between L7 and L12 initializes `lowbits`; nothing constrains `len` or the buffer before L12/L13. 2. **Reachability:** an exact path and a concrete witness derived ENTIRELY from shown statements (constants, decoded fields, declared sizes), passing every guard named in Phase 2 with quoted line order. 3. **Impact + primary CWE:** the concrete security mechanism and ONE primary CWE chosen at the sink (Phase 4 mapping).

static int check_stack_boundary(struct bpf_verifier_env *env, int regno,
				int access_size, bool zero_size_allowed,
				struct bpf_call_arg_meta *meta)
{
	struct bpf_verifier_state *state = env->cur_state;
	struct bpf_reg_state *regs = state->regs;
	int off, i, slot, spi;

	if (regs[regno].type != PTR_TO_STACK) {
		/* Allow zero-byte read from NULL, regardless of pointer type */
		if (zero_size_allowed && access_size == 0 &&
		    register_is_null(regs[regno]))
			return 0;

		verbose(env, "R%d type=%s expected=%s\n", regno,
			reg_type_str[regs[regno].type],
			reg_type_str[PTR_TO_STACK]);
		return -EACCES;
	}

	/* Only allow fixed-offset stack reads */
	if (!tnum_is_const(regs[regno].var_off)) {
		char tn_buf[48];

 		tnum_strn(tn_buf, sizeof(tn_buf), regs[regno].var_off);
 		verbose(env, "invalid variable stack read R%d var_off=%s\n",
 			regno, tn_buf);
		return -EACCES;
 	}
 	off = regs[regno].off + regs[regno].var_off.value;
 	if (off >= 0 || off < -MAX_BPF_STACK || off + access_size > 0 ||
	    access_size < 0 || (access_size == 0 && !zero_size_allowed)) {
		verbose(env, "invalid stack type R%d off=%d access_size=%d\n",
			regno, off, access_size);
		return -EACCES;
	}

	if (env->prog->aux->stack_depth < -off)
		env->prog->aux->stack_depth = -off;

	if (meta && meta->raw_mode) {
		meta->access_size = access_size;
		meta->regno = regno;
		return 0;
	}

	for (i = 0; i < access_size; i++) {
		slot = -(off + i) - 1;
		spi = slot / BPF_REG_SIZE;
		if (state->allocated_stack <= slot ||
		    state->stack[spi].slot_type[slot % BPF_REG_SIZE] !=
			STACK_MISC) {
			verbose(env, "invalid indirect read from stack off %d+%d size %d\n",
				off, i, access_size);
			return -EACCES;
		}
	}
	return 0;
}

Then inventory every security-relevant operation and call with its exact line, including operations hidden inside called functions whose ARGUMENTS (indices, sizes, lengths, pointers, format strings, paths, URLs, queries) are supplied by the shown code:
- memory: reads/writes, copies (memcpy/memmove/strcpy/strncpy/sprintf/sscanf-family/pstrcpy), pointer arithmetic, allocations sized from input, array/container indexing;
- injection: printf-family format strings, system/exec/spawn and shell-command construction (distinguish shell vs exec-argv), SQL/NoSQL/XPath/query construction, log writes (the log sink is the write itself; a downstream backend need not be shown), HTTP header/URL/redirect construction, HTML output, server-side URL consumption (fetch/http client/curl/open/socket/redirect-follow);
